title: Grade XI Physics – Unit 4: Rotational and Circular Motion — Full 80-MCQ Summative Practice
sourceDocument: NBF Grade XI Physics, Unit 4 pp.53–76; FBISE Physics HSSC-I Assessment Framework pp.3–4; Unit 4 SLO audit V38
sourceSection: 56 independent MCQs + 24 self-contained scenario MCQs in 6 complete four-question stimuli; all original SLO-based educational questions grounded in NBF Unit 4
limitations: 80 source-grounded original MCQs are provisional educational practice pending teacher academic and live browser/print review; NOT official FBISE examination questions or an approved answer key.
Scenario items retain full stimulusText per question; they must not be presented without their scenario context if questions are individually shuffled or extracted.
Includes 12 Unit 4 summative theory SLOs only: B-07–B-10 and B-14–B-21; formative B-11 and collision B-12/B-13 are excluded from this chapter.
Options are deliberately balanced to exactly 20 correct answers each for A/B/C/D, with deterministic non-sequential layouts, and explanations for every item.
The 80×0.5=40 mark count is Unit-4-only practice based on the full Section A count. It is not the official board's topic-specific unit allocation.
Public practice is client-side and does not authenticate, write grades, or modify existing student attempts; protected assessments need a separate rollout and permission audit.
Item cognitive tags track the official SLO-level FBISE cognitive categories; a few numerical exercises may need expert teacher classification review before use in formal assessments.

questions.scenarioTitle: Bicycle wheel slowing to rest — NBF Example 4.1
questions.stimulusText: A bicycle tyre of radius 0.331 m rolls without slipping. Initially, its rim speed is 6.80 m/s. It travels 74.8 m before coming to rest with constant angular deceleration. Treat the original rotation direction as positive.

questions.stem: Assuming the tyre rolls without slipping and slows uniformly over the 74.8 m, its angular acceleration is approximately:
questions.explanation: θ = s/r ≈225.98 rad and 0 = ω₀²+2αθ, so α ≈−0.934 rad/s² (≈−0.94).

questions.stem: The approximate time taken by the bicycle tyre to stop is:
questions.explanation: At uniform deceleration, time = 2s/v₀ = (2×74.8)/6.80 = 22.0 s; the textbook reports about 21.9 s using rounded intermediate values.

questions.scenarioTitle: Friction-free banked turn
questions.stimulusText: A 900 kg vehicle travels at constant 12 m/s around a circular bend of radius 50 m. The road is ideally banked and tyre friction is negligible. The normal reaction and weight are the only forces. Take g = 9.8 m/s².

questions.stem: With negligible friction in this banked-road scenario, the horizontal centripetal component is provided by:

options.text: The horizontal component of the road's normal reaction
The vertical component of the normal reaction
A second separate outward applied centrifugal force

questions.explanation: The inclined normal reaction supplies an inward horizontal component; its upward component balances mg.

questions.scenarioTitle: Skater drawing weighted arms inward — angular momentum conservation
questions.stimulusText: An ideal skater has a fixed body moment of inertia of 3.0 kg m² and holds two identical 2.0 kg point masses. Initially each mass is 1.20 m from the axis and the skater rotates at 30 rpm. Both masses are brought inward to radius 0.30 m while the net external axial torque is negligible.

questions.stem: After the skater brings the hand masses inward, the final rotational speed is approximately:
questions.explanation: Iբ = 3 + 2×2×0.30² = 3.36 kg m², and Iᵢωᵢ = Iբωբ, so rpmբ = 30×8.76/3.36 ≈78.2 rpm.

questions.scenarioTitle: Skater drawing weighted arms inward — angular momentum conservation
questions.stimulusText: An ideal skater has a fixed body moment of inertia of 3.0 kg m² and holds two identical 2.0 kg point masses. Initially each mass is 1.20 m from the axis and the skater rotates at 30 rpm. Both masses are brought inward to radius 0.30 m while the net external axial torque is negligible.

questions.stem: During this ideal internal arm movement, the skater's angular momentum about the rotation axis:

options.text: Increases in the same proportion as angular speed
Decreases to half its original value

questions.explanation: With negligible external axial torque, dL/dt = 0, so total axial angular momentum remains constant.

questions.stimulusText: An ideal skater has a fixed body moment of inertia of 3.0 kg m² and holds two identical 2.0 kg point masses. questions.stem: As the skater draws the masses inward, their rotational kinetic energy can increase even though angular momentum is conserved because:

options.text: Internal work is done in moving the masses inward
An external net axial torque must always be present
Rotational kinetic energy is automatically conserved whenever angular momentum is conserved

questions.explanation: Keeping L fixed while reducing I can increase K = L²/(2I); the skater performs internal work.
